summaries.example: Imagine looking at a bright red apple. A representationalist says your visual experience represents the apple as red. If you only hallucinated an apple, your experience could still represent a red apple, even though no real apple is there. The experience would be mistaken, but it could feel similar.
summaries.summary: This entry studies a family of theories about consciousness. These theories say that some conscious experiences are connected to representation: the mind stands for objects, properties, or situations. A belief can represent something real or imaginary, and a perception can be accurate or mistaken. Representationalists apply this idea especially to sensory qualities, such as colors, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. When someone sees a real red apple, the experience may represent the apple’s redness. When someone hallucinates a red apple, the experience may represent redness even though there is no real apple. The theory therefore treats the experienced quality as a represented property rather than as a strange colored object inside the brain. The entry distinguishes weaker and stronger versions. A weak view says sensory states always have representational contents but may also have other kinds of properties. A strong view says the right kind of representation is enough to explain sensory qualities, together with features that make it visual, auditory, or another kind of sensory representation. Philosophers also debate whether these contents depend on the environment, what exactly is represented, and whether the theory reduces consciousness to more basic physical or functional facts. Supporters appeal to the difference between accurate and inaccurate perception, the tendency to notice objects rather than the inner experience itself, and the similarity between perception and hallucination. Critics point to pain, moods, unconscious representation, blurry vision, attention, and cases where experiences seem different even when their contents seem the same. The entry also separates sensory qualities from the higher-order question of what it is like to experience them.
key_ideas: Our minds can represent real things, imaginary things, and situations that are not true.
Representational theories try to explain sensory experiences, such as seeing red or hearing a high note, through representation.
Seeing a real red apple and hallucinating a red apple may have similar experiences, even though only one has a real apple.
Philosophers disagree about whether representation explains all of an experience or only part of it.
Some theories say sensory qualities depend on the world around us; others say they depend only on what is inside the person.
The phrase “what it’s like” can mean a sensory quality itself or the special way a person is aware of that quality.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because it offers one way to connect conscious experience with the world and with the workings of the mind. It also asks whether seeing a color or feeling a pain requires something beyond brain activity and representation. Understanding the debate helps us think carefully about perception, dreams, hallucinations, self-awareness, and the limits of scientific explanations.

important_terms.definition: A mental state being about something, such as believing that a dog is outside or imagining a dragon.
A noticeable sensory feature, such as a color, sound, smell, taste, or feeling of texture.
The part of a mental experience that concerns what it feels like to have it.
A theory saying that sensory experiences have their character partly or wholly because they represent things or properties.

questions_to_think_about: If a person sees a red apple in a dream, is the dream representing something?
Could two people have the same brain state but experience different colors because they are in different environments?
Does a headache represent a problem in a part of the body, or is it simply a painful feeling?
Is seeing red fully explained by representing redness?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya sees a red tomato in good light. Her visual system represents an object as having a certain color, and the experience is veridical if the tomato really has the represented property. Now suppose Noah has a visually indistinguishable hallucination of a tomato. A representationalist can say that Noah’s experience represents a tomato and redness too, but the represented object is nonactual. The challenge is to explain why the representation is visual and conscious rather than merely a linguistic or unconscious representation.
summaries.summary: Representational theories of consciousness attempt to explain certain forms of consciousness in terms of intentionality, understood as representation. The entry distinguishes several uses of “conscious,” including internal awareness, introspection, sensory qualities, and phenomenal consciousness in the sense of what it is like for a subject. Its main focus is the third and fourth forms. A sensory quality is a feature such as experienced redness, a particular pitch, or a taste. The central proposal is that such a quality is a represented property. In veridical perception, a subject may represent the actual color of an object. In hallucination or illusion, the experience may represent an object or property that is not actually present. This allows the theory to avoid treating experience as containing a literal colored object inside the brain. The entry distinguishes pure, strong, and weak forms of the view. Pure representationalism says representation alone is sufficient, but the entry notes that representations occur in many forms, including words and maps. Strong representationalism therefore adds a suitable sensory, functional, or material condition; weak representationalism says only that sensory states necessarily have representational contents. A second distinction concerns narrow versus wide content. On a wide view, environmental features help determine what is represented, so physically similar subjects in different settings might have different sensory qualities. On a narrow view, the relevant contents are fixed internally. Further disputes concern whether experiences represent public physical properties, dispositions, nonactual properties, or Fregean modes of presentation, and whether representationalism reduces phenomenal facts or merely relates them to other,
key_ideas: The entry mainly concerns sensory qualities and the phenomenal question of what an experience is like, while distinguishing these from awareness and introspection.
Representationalists argue that sensory qualities can be understood as represented properties, including properties of hallucinated or otherwise nonactual objects.
Pure representation is not enough: a representation of “red” in speech or writing is not automatically a visual red experience.
Strong and weak representationalism differ over whether suitable representation explains sensory qualities or merely accompanies them.
Narrow and wide representationalism disagree about whether sensory qualities can vary with the subject’s environment, even when internal states are alike.
Representationalists disagree about the contents represented, including physical properties, dispositions, or other kinds of properties, and about whether the theory is reductive or nonreductive.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it connects first-person experience with perception, brain processes, and the external world. If strong representationalism succeeds, sensory qualities may be explained without positing immaterial sense-data or nonphysical properties. If it fails, experiences may contain additional features that representation does not capture. The distinction between sensory qualities and higher-order “what it’s like” properties also shapes arguments about materialism, including knowledge, conceivability, and explanatory-gap arguments. The entry does not settle these disputes; it maps the arguments and the remaining objections.

important_terms.definition: The aboutness of a mental state: a belief, perception, or thought can be directed at an actual or nonactual object, property, or state of affairs.
A sensory property such as experienced redness, pitch, loudness, smell, taste, or texture; this is narrower than every use of “qualia.”
The view that sensory qualities are, or necessarily involve, representational contents of sensory states.
The claim that sensory qualities are represented properties of objects, whether or not those objects actually exist.
The distinction between contents fixed partly by the environment and contents fixed by what is inside the subject.
A strong view that the appropriate kind of representation, together with material or functional features, is sufficient for sensory qualities.
A weaker view that sensory states necessarily represent, while allowing that extra, possibly nonrepresentational properties are involved.
The higher-order property of what an experience is like for its subject, distinguished from the sensory quality experienced.

questions_to_think_about: Does the similarity between perception and hallucination support a common representational explanation, or could it be explained another way?
If an experience represents redness unconsciously, what additional condition would make it a conscious sensory quality?
Would a person transported to an environment with inverted color properties eventually have different sensory qualities?
Can transparency—the tendency to attend to objects rather than experiences—show that sensory qualities are only representational?
Does learning what red looks like involve learning a new fact, or learning a new way to represent a fact already known scientifically?

summaries.example: You look at a picture that can seem to be either a duck or a rabbit. The picture stays the same, but your experience changes when you notice the other animal. A representationalist may say that your mind represents different features or arrangements at different moments. A critic may reply that the picture and its ordinary parts stayed the same, so something about the experience changed without a change in what was represented.
summaries.summary: The entry examines representational theories of consciousness, which explain important kinds of conscious experience through representation. Representation is a way for a mental state to be about an object, property, or situation. A belief can represent a real event, a future event, or something imaginary. Representationalists extend this familiar idea to perception and sensory experience. They argue that experienced redness, a particular sound, or another sensory quality may be a property represented by the mind rather than a special colored or sounded object inside the brain. This approach can treat accurate perception and hallucination in a unified way: in one case the represented object exists, and in the other it does not, while the experiences may still resemble each other. The theory comes in varieties. Pure representationalism would make representation alone sufficient, but the entry emphasizes that words, maps, and signals represent without producing sensory experience. Strong representationalism therefore adds a sensory or functional condition, such as being generated by a visual system and having the right kind of role. Weak representationalism makes the smaller claim that sensory states necessarily have representational contents, while allowing extra properties. Another major issue is whether sensory content is narrow or wide. Wide content depends partly on the subject’s surroundings; narrow content is fixed by what is internal to the subject. This leads to thought experiments involving duplicates and environments with inverted colors. Philosophers also disagree about what is represented: ordinary physical properties, dispositions to cause experiences, nonactual properties, or modes of presentation. The entry presents arguments from materialism, veridicality
key_ideas: Mental representations can be true or false, and they can concern real, imaginary, or absent things.
Representational theories focus especially on sensory qualities and try to explain them as represented properties.
A visual representation must be more than a word or picture: it must be produced in a way connected with vision or a similar sensory system.
Weak representationalism leaves room for extra features of experience; strong representationalism aims to explain sensory qualities through representation and related physical or functional facts.
Wide theories allow the environment to help determine sensory content, while narrow theories hold that relevant content can be shared by internal duplicates.
Objections involve unconscious representations, pain and moods, attention, blurry vision, hallucination, and the possibility of experiences differing despite apparently identical contents.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it asks how ordinary perception connects with consciousness. It may help explain why hallucinations can resemble perception, why we normally attend to objects rather than to our experiences, and why different senses produce different kinds of experience. It also clarifies difficult questions about whether consciousness is entirely physical, whether the outside world partly determines experience, and whether a theory of representation can explain everything that experience contains.

important_terms.definition: When a thought, belief, or experience stands for something or is about something, even if that thing is imaginary.
A sensory feature, such as seeing red, hearing a high pitch, tasting sweetness, or feeling a texture.
A mental state’s being about an object, property, or situation; philosophers often treat this as representation.
The view that sensory experiences get their character from the properties they represent.
A view saying that sensory states have representational content, but that representation may not explain every part of the experience.
A view saying that the right kind of representation, plus suitable sensory or functional features, is enough for a sensory quality.
A dispute over whether the environment helps determine an experience’s content or whether content is fixed inside the person.
The special question of what an experience feels like to the person having it.

questions_to_think_about: When a duck-rabbit picture changes from looking like a duck to looking like a rabbit, what exactly has changed?
Is a hallucination best understood as representing a nonexistent object, or can hallucination be explained without representation?
Could a person represent red without consciously seeing red?
Do pain and anxiety represent bodily or worldly conditions, or are they mainly feelings?
If two people are internally identical but live in different environments, must their visual experiences be identical?
